, at the needle level, O(3) is taken up in a dose-dependent manner, which is determined by the prevailing environmental factors.
O(3)-fluxes are controlled by the same environmental factors as stomatal conductance, and that O(3-)fluxes are not a function of altitude or tree age.
O(3), in contrast to other air pollutants, does not cause any significant injury to trees at the alpine treeline.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

O(3)-induced injury is more likely to occur at sites with higher ambient O(3) concentrations, at higher altitudes, in younger trees and in sun-exposed needles than at sites with lower ambient O(3), at lower altitudes, in older trees, or in shaded needles.
the O(3) dose to the trees depends on the O(3), temperature and irradiance regimes, the stomatal conductance, the needle age and the needle position on the tree.

O(3)-fluxes are mainly controlled by environmental conditions and that O(3)'s impact on the trees is not only dependent on O(3)-concentrations in the air but is also influenced by tree age, needle age and needle position in the crown.
The main takeaway from our work is that
O(3)-induced injury in forest trees may be more severe in the lower canopy and at lower altitudes.
